What are the main GitHub Actions trigger: `push` runs on commits to specified branches - the default for CI on every change. `pull_request` runs against a PR's merge commit, the standard gate before merging. `schedule` (cron syntax) runs on a timer for periodic jobs (nightly builds, scheduled cleanup). `workflow_dispatch` adds a manual 'Run workflow' button in the UI with optional input parameters, for on-demand runs a human triggers deliberately (a manual production deploy). `workflow_call` makes the workflow itself reusable, invokable from another workflow via `uses:`, the mechanism for sharing pipeline logic across repos the way a Jenkins Shared Library or Azure Pipelines template does.
What's the difference between workflow_d: `workflow_dispatch` is triggered by a human clicking 'Run workflow' in the GitHub UI (or via the API/CLI) on that specific repo, with optional typed input fields. `repository_dispatch` is triggered by an external system calling GitHub's API with a custom event type and payload - used when a different system (a webhook from another service, a different CI system, a cron job running elsewhere) needs to programmatically kick off a workflow, rather than a person clicking a button.
How does workflow_call work for reusable: A reusable workflow (defined with `on: workflow_call` and invoked via `uses: org/repo/.github/workflows/file.yml@ref` from a calling workflow's `jobs`) can define multiple jobs, each with its own runner and steps, and can accept both inputs and secrets - suited for sharing an entire multi-job pipeline shape. A composite action bundles a sequence of steps into one reusable unit invoked as a single step within an existing job - suited for a smaller, self-contained sequence (checkout, setup, lint) rather than a whole pipeline's job structure. Choose reusable workflows when you're sharing pipeline shape/orchestration; composite actions when you're sharing a step sequence.
How would you configure a GitHub Actions: Define `on: schedule: - cron: '0 2 * * *'` for a daily 2am UTC run - but be aware GitHub explicitly documents that scheduled workflows can be delayed during periods of high load and aren't guaranteed to run at the exact specified minute, and scheduled workflows are automatically disabled after 60 days of repository inactivity (no commits), which silently breaks a 'set and forget' scheduled job on a low-activity repo unless someone notices and re-enables it - worth explicitly monitoring for scheduled-job execution rather than assuming it's always running.
How would you trigger a GitHub Actions w: Use `repository_dispatch` - the source repo's workflow (or any external caller) makes an authenticated API call to the target repo's dispatch endpoint with a custom event type, and the target repo has a workflow listening for `on: repository_dispatch` with a matching type - this is the standard cross-repo trigger pattern, commonly used when a shared library repo's release should trigger a rebuild in each consuming repo, or a monorepo-adjacent multi-repo setup needs coordinated triggering.
What's the difference between on: pull_r: `pull_request` checks out and runs against the PR's own head branch code, with a restricted, read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN` and no access to repo secrets for PRs from forks - a deliberate security boundary preventing a malicious fork PR from exfiltrating secrets via a modified workflow file. `pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository (with full secret access) but by default still checks out the base branch's code, not the PR's - the danger is a workflow that's modified to explicitly check out and *execute* the PR's own (potentially malicious) code while still running with `pull_request_target`'s elevated secret access, which is a well-known GitHub Actions security anti-pattern to avoid.
How would you use path filters and branc: Combine `on: push: branches: [main] paths: ['services/api/**']` so the workflow only triggers for pushes to `main` that actually touch files under that specific path - critical in a monorepo where you don't want every service's pipeline running on every commit regardless of which service changed. Be aware path filters apply per-event, so a commit touching multiple paths across several filtered workflows correctly triggers all of them, while a commit touching none of a workflow's filtered paths correctly skips it entirely.
What are the different trigger types in: CI triggers (`trigger:`) run on pushes to specified branches, the standard build-on-commit trigger. PR triggers (`pr:`) run against pull requests as a merge validation gate. Scheduled triggers (`schedules:`) run on a cron-like schedule independent of any code change, for periodic jobs. Pipeline triggers (`resources: pipelines:`) let one pipeline trigger automatically when a different, specified pipeline completes successfully - Azure's native mechanism for chaining pipelines together (e.g. a downstream deploy pipeline triggering only after an upstream build pipeline succeeds) without needing an external orchestrator.
How would you configure a pipeline to tr: Declare a `resources: pipelines:` block referencing the upstream pipeline by name/project, with a `trigger:` sub-block specifying which branches of that upstream pipeline's completion should trigger this one - Azure DevOps then automatically starts this pipeline whenever the referenced upstream pipeline finishes successfully on a matching branch, and the current pipeline can also consume the upstream pipeline's build artifacts directly via that same resource reference, without needing to manually re-fetch or re-specify where those artifacts came from.
How do path-based and branch-based trigg: Under `trigger:`, `branches: include/exclude` scope which branches cause a CI trigger, and `paths: include/exclude` further scope it to specific file paths within those branches - functionally the same purpose as GitHub Actions' path filters, letting a monorepo pipeline avoid triggering on changes to unrelated parts of the repo. One Azure-specific nuance: an empty/no-match `paths` filter still evaluates against the full commit's changed files, so a commit touching both an included and excluded path still triggers the pipeline (inclusion wins), which is worth testing explicitly rather than assuming exclude always takes precedence.
What actually triggers a CodePipeline ex: For a CodeCommit source, CodePipeline uses CloudWatch Events (EventBridge) by default for near-instant, event-driven triggering on a new commit. For a GitHub source, CodePipeline can use either a GitHub webhook (near-instant, the recommended modern default) or periodic polling (checking for new commits on an interval, which is slower and was the older default before webhook support existed) - always prefer the webhook/event-driven option where available, since polling adds real latency (minutes, not seconds) between a commit and the pipeline actually starting, and unnecessarily consumes API rate limit checking for changes that usually aren't there.
How would you configure CodePipeline to: Define an EventBridge rule matching a specific event pattern (a CodeCommit push event, an ECR image push, a custom application event) with the target set to start the specific CodePipeline execution - this is useful beyond just the standard source-triggered case, letting you trigger a pipeline from events CodePipeline's built-in source triggers don't natively support (e.g. a new container image landing in ECR from a separate build process, or a custom event from an entirely different system), giving much more flexible event-driven orchestration than CodePipeline's native source-stage triggering alone.
How would you chain multiple CodePipelin: Use an EventBridge rule matching CodePipeline's own pipeline-state-change events (specifically a 'SUCCEEDED' state for the upstream pipeline) with the target set to start the downstream pipeline's execution - this decouples the two pipelines (no direct dependency configured within either pipeline's own definition) while still achieving reliable sequential triggering, and the same EventBridge-based pattern generalizes to triggering pipelines from many other AWS event sources beyond just another pipeline's completion.
Compare how GitHub Actions, Azure Pipeli: GitHub Actions is natively event-driven for its own hosted repos - GitHub's own platform directly dispatches the workflow run the instant a push/PR event occurs, no webhook hop needed since the trigger and the runner are both GitHub-operated. Azure Pipelines similarly uses native, immediate event triggering for Azure Repos, and webhook-based triggering for external sources like GitHub. AWS CodePipeline is event-driven via EventBridge for CodeCommit natively, and webhook-based (the modern default) or polling (the legacy fallback) for external sources like GitHub - the common pattern across all three is that the platform's own native source integration is always event-driven/instant, while connecting to an external source introduces a webhook (fast) or polling (slow) dependency depending on what that integration supports.
How would you debug a workflow/pipeline: Check the trigger configuration's exact scope first - a branch filter, path filter, or event-type mismatch (e.g. `pull_request` configured but the actual event was a `pull_request_target`-eligible fork PR with different default behavior) silently prevents a run without any visible error, since a non-matching trigger simply never starts anything to show an error in. Then check the platform's own webhook delivery log if an external source is involved (GitHub's repo Settings > Webhooks 'Recent Deliveries' view, or the equivalent for Azure DevOps service hooks) to confirm the webhook event was actually received and returned a successful response - a misconfigured or expired webhook (common after a token/secret rotation) will show failed deliveries there even though the triggering event genuinely happened on the source side.
